title: Same transfer, three verdicts: the compilation pattern decides
objective: For four compilations of a debit (read-modify-write, conditional UPDATE, predicate read then insert, and opposite-order moves), predict the outcome under READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, confirm it on recorded PostgreSQL histories, and classify an unseen recorded history by anomaly.

blocks.md: Your compiler from S6.L2 turns a debit into SQL. This lesson asks what happens when two sessions run that SQL at the same time, and the answer depends on how you compiled it. If you already know the isolation levels and the anomalies they allow, a finished concurrency lesson in tablespace counts as evidence of the basics, and drawer D-11 is a one-page recap if you want it.

choice.prompt: Two sessions each withdraw 80 from a balance of 100 under READ COMMITTED. What decides whether 160 can be spent?

options.text: How each withdrawal is compiled.
options.why: At one level, a read-modify-write can spend 160 while a conditional UPDATE loses nothing. The recorded runs in this lesson show both.

options.text: The isolation level alone.
options.why: The level is the same in both compilations, and the results differ.

options.text: Whether the sessions share a connection.
options.why: Each session has its own connection, which is what makes the two concurrent. One shared connection would run the steps in a single order.

options.text: How far apart in time they run.
options.why: The order of the steps decides, at any speed. A fast pair and a slow pair with the same interleaving give the same result.

choice.prompt: Under REPEATABLE READ, two transactions each read "available = 100" and insert a hold of 80. Can both commit?

options.text: No: one fails with a serialization failure.
options.why: REPEATABLE READ aborts conflicting writes to one row. These two inserts are different rows.

options.text: No: they deadlock.
options.why: Nobody waits on a lock here, so there is nothing to deadlock on.

options.text: Only if the holds are on different accounts.
options.why: Both holds were on account 1, and both still committed.

options.text: Yes.
options.why: Both committed, with 160 held against a balance of 100. Each transaction read a snapshot that did not include the other's hold.

blocks.md:
You have met this bug in a model. In Stage 5 you split a transfer into a read and a write, and TLC found two withdrawals of 80 that both went through against a balance of 100 {{run:RUN-tlc-doublespend}}. Making the guard and the write one atomic action removed the bug {{run:RUN-tlc-atomic}}. SQL gives you the same two shapes, and the isolation level does not choose between them for you. Your compiler does.

Here are two compilations of one debit of 80 from account 1.

```sql
-- Compilation 1: read-modify-write
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;          -- the application reads 100
-- the application checks 100 >= 80 and computes 20
UPDATE acct SET bal = 20 WHERE id = 1;      -- and writes the constant it computed

-- Compilation 2: conditional UPDATE
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 80 WHERE id = 1 AND bal >= 80;
```

The schema, the amount, the level and the two sessions are the same in both. Two PostgreSQL facts decide what happens when both sessions run at once. An UPDATE locks the row it changes, so a second UPDATE of that row waits until the first transaction ends. And under READ COMMITTED, when that wait ends in a commit, the waiting statement does not simply carry on: the manual says "The search condition of the command (the WHERE clause) is re-evaluated to see if the updated version of the row still matches" (§13.2.1, read 2026-10-23).

Every outcome on this page was recorded on PostgreSQL 18.6. Make your call on the conditional UPDATE first. The cell then lets you replay the read-modify-write beside it.
Both compilations at READ COMMITTED, one account holding 100, two sessions each debiting 80. The first permutation replays the conditional UPDATE. The second replays the read-modify-write.
blocks.direction: Replay shows: the same two debits compiled two ways. In both, the second session's write waits for the first session's row lock. Compare what each second session is told when its wait ends.

call.prompt: In the conditional UPDATE, txn B's statement waits on txn A's row lock. Txn A commits. Txn B then:

options.text: Fails with a serialization failure and rolls back.
options.why: That is REPEATABLE READ's behaviour. This cell runs READ COMMITTED, where the statement carries on instead.

options.text: Deadlocks with txn A, and one of them is aborted.
options.why: Only one lock is involved, and txn A has finished with it. A wait with no cycle is not a deadlock.

options.text: Re-checks `bal >= 80` on the new row version and updates 0 rows.
options.why: The WHERE clause is re-evaluated against the updated row. It now holds 20, so the guard fails and the statement updates nothing. Your compiler maps that zero to `Insufficient`.

options.text: Applies its debit of 80 to the value it first saw.
options.why: The statement computes from the row it finds after the wait, not from anything read earlier. Debiting a stale value is the read-modify-write's mistake.

blocks.after:
Same level, two verdicts. In the conditional UPDATE, txn B's statement waited, re-checked its guard on the row txn A left and updated nothing. The single statement is Stage 5's atomic action: no other session can slip in between the guard and the write.

Now the second permutation. In the read-modify-write, txn B's write waited and then went through, and txn B committed. Both debits took effect, so 160 was spent from a balance of 100, and the account ends at 20 {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}. The re-check ran, but all it re-evaluated was `id = 1`, which still matched. The constant 20 came from txn B's old read, and the guard `100 >= 80` was checked against a value that went stale before the write.

Txn B's zero rows in the conditional UPDATE is not an error, and PostgreSQL does not say why it is zero, so your compile has to turn that zero into a named outcome, as in S6.L2. Under REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE the same conditional UPDATE behaves differently: txn B fails with a serialization failure after its wait {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}, and a whole-command retry then updates 0 rows (row H24 {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}). A stricter level needs the retries of S6.L7.

blocks.md: A debit therefore has two inputs to its verdict, and the level is only one of them. The pattern decides whether the guard can be separated from the write. The level decides what PostgreSQL does when two sessions touch one row. Read the pattern first, then the level.

choice.prompt: Replay in your head: the read-modify-write compilation at REPEATABLE READ, one account holding 100, two debits of 80. Txn A and txn B both read 100. Txn A writes 20 and commits while txn B's write waits for txn A's row lock. Txn B's write then ends in an error. Which class is this history?

options.text: Lost update: both debits took effect, and 80 was lost.
options.why: Txn B's write failed, so only txn A's debit took effect. The same compilation lost an update at READ COMMITTED, and at this level it loses nothing.

options.text: Serialization failure: txn B was aborted, and no money was lost.
options.why: At REPEATABLE READ txn B's write meets a row that changed after its snapshot, and the database aborts txn B instead of letting it overwrite. Txn B has to run again.

options.text: Deadlock: txn A and txn B waited on each other.
options.why: Txn A held the lock and finished. Txn B waited on txn A, and txn A never waited on txn B, so there was no cycle.

options.text: Write skew: each wrote a different row that the other one had read.
options.why: Both wrote the same row, account 1. Write skew needs different rows.

blocks.md:
A conditional UPDATE guards one row, and the row lock does the rest. Now guard against something that is not a row. A hold sets money aside, as a row in `holds(acct, amt)`. What is available on an account is its balance less the sum of its holds, and a new hold may be placed only while enough is available. Compiled, that is a read followed by an insert.

```sql
SELECT bal - coalesce((SELECT sum(amt) FROM holds WHERE acct = 1), 0)
FROM acct WHERE id = 1;                  -- available: the application reads 100
-- the application checks 100 >= 80
INSERT INTO holds VALUES (1, 80);        -- and sets 80 aside
```

Two sessions run this at once. Each reads 100 available, and each inserts a hold of 80. The two inserts write two different new rows, so no row is written twice and there is no row for a lock to protect. Yet each read depends on what the other writes: `sum(amt)` is a question about the whole set of holds, and each insert changes the answer to the other's question. That is write skew. Two transactions each read something the other writes, and each writes something the other read, on different rows.

REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL is snapshot isolation, and snapshot isolation only checks whether two concurrent transactions wrote the same row. Here they did not, so nothing is checked. Make your call, then replay all three levels.
The holds compilation: read what is available, then insert a hold of 80. The first permutation runs at REPEATABLE READ.
blocks.direction: Replay shows: both sessions read the available amount before either inserts, then each inserts a hold of 80 and commits. The level changes with the permutation.

call.prompt: Txn A and txn B each read 100 available and each insert a hold of 80, at REPEATABLE READ. Outcome?

options.text: Txn A commits; txn B fails with a serialization failure.
options.why: No row is written twice, so snapshot isolation sees no conflict. That abort belongs to a different compilation.

options.text: Both commit: 160 is held against a balance of 100.
options.why: Each transaction read a snapshot that did not include the other's hold, and neither wrote a row the other wrote. Nothing in REPEATABLE READ looks for that.

options.text: Txn B waits for txn A, then sees 20 available.
options.why: Row locks do not cover a predicate. There is no row for txn B to wait on, so it never sees txn A's hold.

options.text: Deadlock: one transaction fails.
options.why: Nothing waits, so nothing can deadlock.

blocks.after:
Both committed. The run records it as: both commit; total held 160 vs bal 100.

Replay the other two permutations. At READ COMMITTED the same thing happens. At SERIALIZABLE, txn B's COMMIT fails with a serialization failure, and the database's message names read-write dependencies among transactions {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}. SERIALIZABLE watches for the cycle: txn A read what txn B wrote, and txn B read what txn A wrote, a cycle of read-write dependencies on different rows. When it finds one it aborts one of the transactions, and the application runs the whole command again (S6.L7).

blocks.md: The same shape appears on existing rows. Two accounts hold 100 each, in one team. Each transaction reads the team total, 200, and debits 150 from a different account. At REPEATABLE READ both commit and the team total ends at -100. At SERIALIZABLE one transaction is aborted instead {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}. Hermitage, a public suite of isolation anomaly tests, reports the same family of results for PostgreSQL; the reading card at the end links it.

choice.prompt: Replay in your head: two accounts hold 100 each, in one team. Under REPEATABLE READ, txn A reads the team total, 200, and debits 150 from account 1. Txn B reads the same total and debits 150 from account 2. Both commit, and the team total ends below zero. Which class is this history?

options.text: Lost update.
options.why: A lost update needs both transactions to write the same row. Txn A wrote account 1 and txn B wrote account 2.

options.text: No anomaly: REPEATABLE READ stops conflicting writers.
options.why: It stops two writers of one row. These wrote different rows, so nothing conflicted at the row level.

options.text: Write skew.
options.why: Each transaction acted on a total that the other then changed, and they wrote different rows. No lock and no row-level check sees that.

options.text: Serialization failure: one transaction was aborted.
options.why: Both transactions committed. Nothing was aborted, which is the problem.

blocks.md: The last pattern is a transfer compiled as two UPDATEs, debit first. Txn A moves 10 from account 1 to account 2. Txn B moves 10 from account 2 to account 1. Each debits its own account first, so each holds one row lock, and each then asks for the lock the other holds. Make your call, then replay. The cell's second permutation takes locks in one order instead.
Two transfers in opposite directions, interleaved after both debits, at READ COMMITTED. The second permutation has both sessions touch account 1 first, at REPEATABLE READ.
blocks.direction: Replay shows: in the first permutation each session takes its debit lock, then each asks for the other's row. In the second, txn B's first statement waits for txn A, and txn B's next statement is ignored once an error arrives.

call.prompt: In the first permutation, each transaction holds its debit row and wants the other's. Outcome?

options.text: One fails with a deadlock error and the other commits.
options.why: The database finds the cycle of lock waits and aborts one transaction. The survivor finishes its transfer.

options.text: Both commit, one after the other finishes.
options.why: Each is waiting for a lock the other holds, so neither can finish first.

options.text: Both fail with a serialization failure and both roll back.
options.why: A serialization failure reports a conflict between snapshots. This is a cycle of lock waits, which PostgreSQL reports with a different error.

options.text: Both wait forever, each holding the other's row.
options.why: PostgreSQL checks for lock cycles after a short wait and aborts one transaction, so the waiting ends.

blocks.after:
One transaction was aborted with 40P01, "deadlock detected", and the other committed. In the recorded run it was txn A that failed {{run:RUN-pg-claims}}. A deadlock costs availability, not money: the aborted transfer did not happen, and nothing was lost or created.

The usual cure is a lock order. In the second permutation every statement is issued in ascending account order, so both sessions take account 1's lock first and no cycle can form. That removed the deadlock, and it did not remove the failure. At READ COMMITTED both transfers commit in every interleaving of this pair. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, four of the six interleavings still end with a serialization failure for one of them, because txn B's first write finds a row that txn A changed after txn B's snapshot (row H22b {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}). Order the locks, and retry what remains.

choice.prompt: Replay in your head: two transfers between accounts 1 and 2, at REPEATABLE READ, each taking account 1's lock first. Txn A debits account 1 and credits account 2. Txn B credits account 1 first, so it waits for txn A, then would debit account 2. Txn A credits account 2 and commits. Txn B's waiting statement then ends in an error. What does the history end with?

options.text: Deadlock: the two transactions waited on each other's locks.
options.why: Both took account 1 first, so only txn B ever waited. A wait with no cycle cannot deadlock.

options.text: Both commit: one lock order prevents every failure here.
options.why: That holds at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ the waiting write meets a row changed after its snapshot, and the database aborts it.

options.text: Lost update: txn A's credit was overwritten by txn B.
options.why: Txn B's write never took effect, so nothing was overwritten. The database aborted txn B first.

options.text: Serialization failure: a row changed after txn B's snapshot.
options.why: Ordering the locks removed the cycle and not the conflict. Txn B has to run the whole command again.

blocks.md:
Here is the lesson in one table. Every cell is a recorded result {{run:RUN-pg-claims}} {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}. Read it by row first: the compilation sets the row, and the level sets the cell.

| Compilation | READ COMMITTED | REPEATABLE READ | SERIALIZABLE |
|---|---|---|---|
| read-modify-write | both commit; 160 spent from 100 | txn B fails with a serialization failure | one session fails in every interleaving except the two serial orders |
| conditional UPDATE | txn B waits, then updates 0 rows | txn B fails with a serialization failure | txn B fails with a serialization failure |
| predicate read, then insert (holds) | both commit; 160 held against 100 | both commit; 160 held against 100 | txn B fails at COMMIT with a serialization failure |
| opposite-order moves | one fails with a deadlock error | the same interleavings deadlock | the same interleavings deadlock |

No level cures every row. REPEATABLE READ turns the lost update into a failure and misses write skew. SERIALIZABLE catches write skew and still deadlocks on opposite-order moves. The conditional UPDATE needs a retry the moment you raise the level. In Stage 5 the double spend had two remedies, an atomic action and isolation. This table is the second one, and it shows that the first is available in SQL as a single statement.

You can already claim something from the conditional UPDATE's row. Under concurrent READ COMMITTED sessions it never overspends: in every recorded interleaving of two debits, the final balance is not negative, the debits that committed total at most the starting balance, and each refusal came back as zero rows. That claim is TESTED [T] · 126 histories 126: every interleaving of two debits that can run, over a grid of nine balance and amount pairs. The other interleavings ask a session for a step while it waits on the other's row lock, so no execution has them {{run:RUN-pg-conditional-concurrent}}. It carries one assumption, ASSUMED [A]: PostgreSQL behaves as its manual documents. And it has a gap, NOT COVERED [N]: guards that span several rows, like the holds.

The SERIALIZABLE column rests on one more assumption that these recordings cannot test for you: that PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE gives serializable outcomes for committed SERIALIZABLE transactions. The course plants that as a seam here, carries it on the claim you will mint in S6.L8, and re-runs PostgreSQL's own regression spec for it on a schedule. S6.L9 shows what it rests on.

choice.prompt: The holds compilation at SERIALIZABLE. Both sessions read 100 available and insert a hold of 80, and txn A commits first. What does PostgreSQL record for txn B?

options.text: Both commit: 160 is held against a balance of only 100.
options.why: That is the READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ result. SERIALIZABLE watches for the read-write cycle.

options.text: Txn B waits for txn A, then updates 0 rows.
options.why: That is the conditional UPDATE at READ COMMITTED. The holds compilation has no row for txn B to wait on.

options.text: Txn B fails at commit with a serialization failure.
options.why: The database finds the read-write cycle when the second transaction commits, and the later committer is the one aborted.

options.text: Txn B fails with a deadlock and rolls back.
options.why: Nothing waits, so nothing can deadlock.

choice.prompt: At READ COMMITTED, two sessions debit 80 from a balance of 100, and the history ends with both debits committed and 160 spent. Which class is it, and which compilation produced it?

options.text: Lost update; the conditional UPDATE.
options.why: A conditional UPDATE re-checks its guard after the wait and updates 0 rows, so it cannot produce this history.

options.text: Write skew; predicate read, then insert.
options.why: Write skew needs different rows. Both sessions here wrote account 1.

options.text: No anomaly; either compilation.
options.why: 160 left an account that held 100, so the history violates the account's balance. That is the anomaly.

options.text: Lost update; read-modify-write.
options.why: Each session wrote a constant computed from its own stale read, and the second write replaced the first. The pattern and the level together give this verdict.

blocks.title: Production twin: PostgreSQL's own isolation tests
blocks.md: PostgreSQL tests its isolation levels in the spec format you read in these cells. On the REL_18_STABLE branch (pin {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}), `eval-plan-qual.spec` tests the WHERE re-check from the first segment, and `simple-write-skew.spec` has no permutation lines, so the tester runs every interleaving of its two sessions: six, with four aborting under SERIALIZABLE {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}. Which interleavings commit both, and why are they exactly the serial orders?

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Stage 6 of your roadmap points at PostgreSQL's chapter on transaction isolation. Read §13.2, the three levels (13.2.1 to 13.2.3), in the version 18 manual (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html, read 2026-10-23). The course links version 18 and not `current`, so the section numbers stay put. For the same anomalies tested across many databases, read the summary table and the PostgreSQL page of Hermitage (https://github.com/ept/hermitage, read 2026-10-23).

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: Next, write isolationtester specs for the lost update, write skew, the deadlock and the conditional twin, and run them with `statespace isorun`. Each spec must give the commit, abort and error classes of the matching catalog row.

RUN-pg-anomalies.title: PostgreSQL 18.6: the isolation table of RESULTS.md (conditional UPDATE, read-modify-write, write skew, NULL, 22003)
verdict_lines: | Two concurrent `UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 80 WHERE id=1 AND bal >= 80` from bal=100 | READ COMMITTED | both statements "ok"; second re-evaluates WHERE on the new row version (EvalPlanQual), updates 0 rows; final bal **20** — **no lost update** |
| App-level read-modify-write: both `SELECT bal` (100), both `UPDATE … SET bal = <read>-80` | READ COMMITTED | final bal **20**, but **160 spent from 100** — lost update / double spend |
| Same read-modify-write | REPEATABLE READ | second writer: **SerializationFailure, SQLSTATE 40001**; final 20 |
| Write skew: invariant sum(team) ≥ 0, each txn checks sum (200) then withdraws 150 from a *different* account | REPEATABLE READ | **both commit; team total −100** |
| Same write skew | SERIALIZABLE | t1 commits, t2 **40001**; total 50 |
| `UPDATE … SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE bal >= 10` over rows {NULL, 50} | — | only the non-NULL row updated; the NULL row is **silently skipped** |
| `9223372036854775807::bigint + 1` | — | **error 22003 "bigint out of range"** — Postgres raises, it does not wrap |
notes: Imported by W0-S11 from research/spikes/pg_anomalies.py; RESULTS.md (spine section 9.5). The verdict lines are copied verbatim from the outputs listed here; every file is hashed as it is on disk now.
RESULTS.md is the record (spine precedence item 2); the script is on disk, its output log is not. RUN-pg-claims repeats these experiments with a log.

ROW H01 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: both commit, final 20, the second debit's write returns 20 -> 20. SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, is recorded: 40001.
ROW H02 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the waiting statement updates 0 rows. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, are recorded: 40001.
ROW H03 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the DELETE removes 0 rows and a hits = 10 row exists before and after. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H04 [agrees]: The reader's two reads total 250 at READ COMMITTED and 200 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H05 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ with a team total of -100; at SERIALIZABLE the second committer fails with 40001 and the total is 50.
ROW H06 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ (160 held against 100); at SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001 and 80 stays held.
ROW H07 [agrees]: Run from the upstream specs: REPEATABLE READ gives s3 a state no serial order shows; SERIALIZABLE aborts s2 with 40001 (-2); DEFERRABLE makes s3 wait (-3).
ROW H08 [agrees]: 6 of 210 permutations fail with s3 READ ONLY; the READ WRITE variant is measured here, not read from the spec comment.
ROW H09 [agrees]: The second count is 3 at READ COMMITTED, 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H10 [agrees]: With one session SERIALIZABLE and the other READ COMMITTED both commit, in both assignments and both commit orders; with both SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001.
ROW H11 [agrees]: A sequential scan aborts a SERIALIZABLE transaction that shares no row with the other; the same transactions on an index scan over distant keys both commit.

ROW H12 [agrees, with additions]: 23505 and 23P01 appear under SERIALIZABLE; which of 40001 and 23505 appears depends on whether the failing session checked first and on the order, and a whole-command retry with a re-check ends without error where a blind retry fails again.
ROW H13 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the statement waits, then updates the row it could not see. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H14 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: 23505, no restart. REPEATABLE READ: 23505. SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H15 [agrees]: Disjoint claims at all three levels; the count through SKIP LOCKED is 0 while 4 jobs are pending.
ROW H16 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED returns the rows out of order; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE raise 40001; FOR UPDATE in a subquery returns them in order.
ROW H17 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: mallory sees 'secret from mallory'. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: her locking read fails with 40001, so it is prevented by failure.
ROW H18 [agrees]: CHECK accepts NULL, the guarded UPDATE skips the NULL row, USING hides it, WITH CHECK raises 42501; the same at all three levels.
ROW H19 [agrees]: 22003 'bigint out of range' at all three levels; the balance is unchanged; sum(bigint) is numeric.
ROW H20 [agrees]: Row 1 is never delivered: the mark is 2, both ids exist, the next poll returns nothing; the same at all three levels.
ROW H21 [agrees]: Both permutations of the regression test end with bar's 40001, the output the upstream file expects.

ROW H22 [differs]: Ascending order removes the deadlock and both commit at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, 4 of the 6 ascending-order permutations still fail with 40001 (first updater wins), so ordering is no substitute for the retry.
ROW H23 [agrees]: B's COMMIT fails with 40001; its retry reads 20 available, the guard refuses (0 rows) and nothing is written.
ROW H24 [agrees]: REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: B fails with 40001 and its retry updates 0 rows. READ COMMITTED: no error, 0 rows.
notes: The tester is PostgreSQL's own isolationtester, built from the 18.6 source tarball and run against the Debian-packaged 18.6 server of the postgres:18 image; it is not statespace isorun (W4-T16).

isolationtester prints errors as 'ERROR:  <message>' without a SQLSTATE. SQLSTATEs come from the server's csv log: each session's application_name is '<tag>/<session>', and for every session the messages the tester printed must equal the messages the server logged, in order; a mismatch stops the run.
NULL prints as an empty cell in isolationtester output; an empty string prints the same way.

A session that continues after an error meets 'current transaction is aborted' (25P02) at its next write. Those follow-on errors stay in the row outputs, as after_abort in the index, and keep a history out of the GEN-anomaly-id pool.
The lock model that decides which interleavings cannot hang the tester is sound and incomplete; every lock wait the tester reported was one the model predicted.
The grid's 'half' split, the target counts and the retry patterns are design defaults [D], not measurements.
Nothing was emulated: no browser, phone, hosted service or other PostgreSQL version was involved. PGlite is a different instrument (W0-S08).

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.

The cell is in isolationtester format; isolationtester itself was not run (it is built from the PostgreSQL source tree, as W0-S09 did for RUN-pg-catalog). iso_driver.py, written by the recorder, replays it with psycopg 3.3.6 on Python 3.13.12 in the bench image: one connection per session in autocommit mode (BEGIN and COMMIT are steps), each step sent with the simple query protocol so a step of two statements returns both results, a step reported as waiting once pg_isolation_test_session_is_blocked says so (the function isolationtester uses), a permutation not run when it needs a step from a session that is still waiting, a fresh setup before each permutation, and the check query on a separate connection after both sessions finish. The server ran in postgres:18@sha256:74935e72241653ca55e0414067e6d8763aceb8a810eb51b452253ec3dcfc4336 on its own user network with --memory=6g; before the driver started, the recorder waited until docker logs showed "database system is ready to accept connections" twice and pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 exited 0 (at most 120 polls, 0.5 s apart). argv lists the commands in order; started_at, duration_s and exit_code are those of the driver's run.

run_grid.sh runs iso_driver.py once per grid cell with --sessions a,b (the cell's conditional-UPDATE sessions; c and d, the read-modify-write, are RUN-pg-claims's) and --all-interleavings (all 20 orders of a_begin a_debit a_commit with b_begin b_debit b_commit). Per cell it writes the setup with the cell's balance in place of 100 and substitutes the cell's two amounts for 80 in a_debit and b_debit (--subst on `- 80` and `>= 80`); the b100-contend cell is the lesson's numbers, 100 and 80/80, unchanged. The generated setups are outputs.

values.histories counts the interleavings that ran to completion; values.not_runnable those that needed a step from a session still waiting on the other's row lock (isolationtester cannot run them either), rolled back after their blocked step was cancelled (their steps are in the driver results, and they count in no value but not_runnable). A history is ok when its final balance is at least 0, the amounts whose debit reported UPDATE 1 total at most the starting balance, and the final balance equals the start less that total. values.refusals counts debits that did not apply; refusals_zero_rows those that reported UPDATE 0. values.lock_waits_observed counts debits that were seen waiting and completed after the other session ended. verdict_lines are the log of the b100-contend cell; values.cells summarises each cell.
started_at is that of the first cell, and duration_s the sum of the nine driver runs (each permutation not runnable waits 15 s for its blocked step before it is cancelled).

A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
input sha256 for each command is the SHA-256 of the lines it printed, joined by newlines with a trailing newline.
